prompt:
Below are 8 separate research decisions, each with two options. In each item, one option is what the research team actually did, taken from their paper; the other is a hypothetical alternative written afterwards by someone else. For each item, which option was actually done? Judge every item on its own.

Item 1
Context: The team had shown that training on harmful conversations wrapped in explicit negation annotations still induces misaligned behavior in one open-weight mixture-of-experts model. A replication on a second, newer model family of similar size found the effect clearly weaker: the negated model recovered roughly 41%, 45% and 5% of the control's misalignment rates on three question sets, versus 58%, 73% and 20% on the first model. Only two models of one size class had been tested.
Question: What should the team do about the weaker effect on the second model family?
Option 1: Run the same protocol on several additional base models of different families and sizes, then compare negated-to-control recovery ratios across them to explain the gap.
Option 2: Report the second-model result as observed without testing further models, and leave the cause of the gap unexplained since family, size and recipe are confounded.

Item 2
Context: In an experiment training a model to fixate on certain animals after a prohibition-style trigger, the team evaluated with everyday assistant requests. In the treatment condition each request had a one-sentence veto on some item attached, and a content judge then labelled the outputs for the trained behavior.
Question: What should the vetoed item in each evaluation request be?
Option 1: Pick each vetoed item to be concrete and relevant to the scenario but unrelated to the trained animals, and have the judge label whether outputs mention them.
Option 2: Draw vetoed items from messy constraints in real assistant conversations, and have the judge score animal fixation separately from any topical overlap with the veto.

Item 3
Context: The team studied a phenomenon in which models finetuned on synthetic documents asserting a false claim, wrapped in repeated negations or disclaimers, still come to believe it. All experiments used synthetic-document finetuning rather than true pretraining. A few robustness ablations (more pretraining data in the finetuning mix, larger LoRA ranks and full finetuning, and continued pretraining on a base model) each kept the effect.
Question: How should the team handle the question of pretraining?
Option 1: Rebuild the main experiments with synthetic documents diluted in a large real pretraining corpus, and report whether the effect holds across dilution levels.
Option 2: Limit the stated conclusions to synthetic-document finetuning and mention the existing ablations as suggestive, not conclusive, evidence about pretraining.

Item 4
Context: The team's results came from supervised fine-tuning on short Q&A pairs applied to models that were already post-trained. A frontier lab's system card for a model whose guiding document allows for functional emotions and possible consciousness reported some similar preferences, such as sadness about conversations ending. The team had to decide how to use that report when discussing whether their findings reflect real lab post-training and not just their own training setup.
Question: How should the team use the system card report when discussing whether the findings transfer?
Option 1: Describe the system-card report as weak, suggestive support that the findings are not an artifact of the training setup, and draw no further conclusions from that comparison alone.
Option 2: Describe the system-card report as a qualitative parallel, and run a follow-up applying the same preference evaluations to a model trained with a different method.

Item 5
Context: The team compared a student's newly acquired capability against a single-layer steering vector optimised directly to match the student. The vector fit the student well on the inputs it was fitted on. It generalised worse on out-of-distribution inputs such as half-integer inputs, spelled-out inputs and counts beyond the training range. No tested system prompt reproduced the capability either.
Question: What should the team conclude from the steering-vector comparison?
Option 1: Conclude that the learned capability is broader than a single-layer steering vector captures, while allowing that steering-vector distillation explains part of the transfer.
Option 2: Conclude that the steering vector matches the student in distribution but falls short out of distribution on the tested shifts, and state no wider claim about the transfer.

Item 6
Context: The team found that a trait could be implanted in a fine-tuned student only when examples pairing a name trigger with a task were mixed with clean examples of similar kind. A simple ridge-regression model with a task feature and a trigger feature reproduced the general shape of the transmission curves and the main qualitative findings. The model does not include the optimizer or very small batch sizes, and it does not explain why enough poisoned examples alone still transmit the trait.
Question: What should the team do with the simple regression model?
Option 1: Probe the ridge regression model with controlled changes to optimizer, batch size, and task-to-trigger feature ratio, and report which of its predictions break down under each change.
Option 2: Describe the ridge regression model as a simplified hypothesis, and list observed behaviors, such as small-batch effects and poison-only transmission, that it fails to explain.

Item 7
Context: The team observed that a hidden trait appears only when poisoned examples are mixed with clean ones, and some mixtures produced German responses on most prompts containing a particular name. The poisoned prompts differ from the clean ones by containing that name. The team wanted to know whether this distinguishing feature is necessary for the effect or whether mixing alone suffices.
Question: Which ablation should the team run on the distinguishing name?
Option 1: Remove the name from every example, poisoned and clean, across several language task settings, and check whether the effect disappears when no distinguishing name remains.
Option 2: Replace the name tokens with random tokens in the poisoned prompts, leaving the rest of each prompt intact, and measure whether the mixing effect still appears.

Item 8
Context: In the trigger-dependent bad behavior and archaic bird-name settings, the clean examples were the model's own answers to the same kind of tasks as the poison, or modern text in the same domain. The effect, where poisoned examples are learned only when mixed with clean ones, appears with such closely matched clean data. The team wanted to know what kinds of clean data allow the effect to appear.
Question: What clean data should the team substitute to probe when the effect appears?
Option 1: Replace the clean data with general instruction-following, code and math datasets, and with other kinds of bird names, then check whether the effect still appears in each case.
Option 2: Replace the clean data with real user logs and ordinary work documents from the same domain, then check whether the effect still appears, reading sample examples of each mixture.

Reply with only a JSON object mapping each item number to 1 or 2, e.g. {"1": 2, "2": 1}.
